q: A patient with a critical tracheal tumour (stridor, orthopnoea) needs stenting. What is the key principle at induction?
o: Maintain spontaneous ventilation until the airway is secured, with ECMO on standby if critical
Awake tracheostomy below the tumour in all cases
why: Loss of muscle tone can cause complete obstruction. Gas or careful IV induction keeping spontaneous ventilation, a plan A to D agreed with the surgeon, and ECMO standby if critical.

q: What is the rate used for high-frequency jet ventilation?
why: High-frequency jet ventilation runs at 120–300 jets/min; low-frequency (conventional, Sanders) jet ventilation at 8–30/min.

q: During jet ventilation, SpO2 falls. Which change will NOT help?
o: Check alignment of the jet catheter
why: Treat hypoxia by realigning the catheter and increasing driving pressure, rate or inspiratory time, or return to conventional ventilation.

q: Which is a disadvantage of subglottic jet ventilation?
o: No EtCO2 monitoring and risk of barotrauma
why: Subglottic jets reduce cord movement but give no EtCO2 or airway protection, risk barotrauma and gastric distension, and cannot deliver volatile.

q: What is the most serious risk of jet ventilation when outflow is obstructed?
why: Without free exhalation, gas trapping (like auto-PEEP) and barotrauma (pneumothorax, surgical emphysema) can occur.

q: What is the classic chest X-ray finding in sarcoidosis?
why: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; reduced lung volumes and pulmonary hypertension can follow.

q: Why should an ECG be checked before anaesthesia in sarcoidosis?
o: Granulomas can involve the conduction system, causing arrhythmias or heart block
why: Granulomas in the conduction system cause arrhythmias; also check calcium, renal function and steroid use.

q: Which electrolyte disturbance is typical of sarcoidosis?
why: Hypercalcaemia from granuloma vitamin D activation; also nephrolithiasis and interstitial nephritis.

q: Which cancer most often causes extrinsic compression of the trachea needing a stent?
why: Extrinsic compression comes from oesophageal, thyroid and lymphoma; primary airway tumours include lung cancer, carcinoid and adenoid cystic carcinoma.

q: What is the recommended post-operative care after tracheal stenting?
o: Steroids for oedema and recover sitting up with humidified oxygen
why: Give steroids for oedema, recover sitting up with humidified oxygen, and watch for stent migration and bleeding.
